articles.title: The best ways to stay cool on a motorcycle this summer - Visordown

articles.full_text:
A warm summer's day and an empty road are about as close to motorcycling perfection as it gets. But when temperatures start pushing towards 30°C and beyond, riding a motorcycle can become uncomfortable surprisingly quickly.
The problem isn't just that you're hot. Dehydration, fatigue and heat exhaustion can all affect your concentration, reactions and decision-making, which is rather important when you're sitting on a motorcycle surrounded by other road users.
That doesn't mean you need to put the bike away whenever the mercury rises. There are plenty of simple things you can do to stay cool while riding a motorcycle in hot weather, without compromising your protective gear or making yourself miserable.
1. Drink before you're thirsty
If you're heading out for a long ride on a hot day, hydration should be part of your preparation rather than something you think about once you're already thirsty.
Riding in the heat, particularly in full motorcycle gear, means you can lose a surprising amount of fluid. You might not notice it while you're concentrating on the road, but the effects of dehydration can creep up on you and leave you feeling tired, sluggish or unable to concentrate properly.
Carry plenty of water and drink regularly throughout the ride. A hydration pack is particularly useful because you can drink little and often without having to wait until your next fuel stop.
It's also worth drinking before you set off. If you're already dehydrated when you climb onto the bike, you're starting the ride on the back foot.
2. Take more breaks than usual
There's no prize for completing a motorcycle journey without stopping. In hot weather, regular breaks are one of the easiest ways to keep yourself comfortable and alert. Find somewhere shady, take your helmet off, get some water down you and give your body a chance to cool down before carrying on.
If it's particularly hot, stopping roughly every hour is a reasonable starting point, although the right interval will depend on the conditions, your route and how you're feeling.
A five or ten-minute break might seem like wasted riding time, but it's considerably better than pushing on until you're exhausted and struggling to concentrate.
3. Wear motorcycle gear, not less gear
When the temperature climbs, it's tempting to leave the jacket at home, ditch the gloves or head out in shorts and a T-shirt.
Don't.
Apart from the obvious consequences if you come off, riding without proper protective equipment isn't necessarily going to make you feel better. Good motorcycle gear is designed to protect you while also managing airflow and moisture, particularly if you choose equipment designed specifically for summer riding.
A well-ventilated motorcycle jacket, mesh panels and a breathable base layer can make a huge difference. The same applies to your trousers, boots, gloves and helmet.
You don't need to choose between staying cool and staying protected. Choose the right gear instead.
4. Use every vent you've got
Your motorcycle gear has vents for a reason, so use them. Open the ventilation points on your jacket and trousers, and make sure your helmet vents are open when conditions allow. The airflow you get once you're moving can make a significant difference, particularly compared with sitting in still air while wearing several layers of protective equipment.
Just remember that ventilation works best when you're actually moving. Which brings us neatly to the next problem.
5. Avoid the hottest part of the day
If you're planning a long motorcycle ride during a period of very hot weather, think about when you're going to ride rather than simply where you're going.
The middle of the day is usually the toughest period, when air and road-surface temperatures are at their highest. Setting off early in the morning can make a surprisingly big difference, and you'll often have quieter roads to enjoy at the same time.
Alternatively, wait until later in the afternoon or evening when temperatures start to fall.
There's also something particularly satisfying about an early-morning motorcycle ride. You get cooler air, quieter roads and don't have to spend the first few hours of the day cooking inside your riding gear.
6. Keep moving where you safely can
There's a reason sitting in stationary traffic on a motorcycle when it's 30°C feels so much worse than cruising along an open road.
Moving air helps carry heat away from your body, while sitting in a queue leaves you exposed to direct sunlight with little or no airflow. Your motorcycle is also producing plenty of heat of its own, which isn't particularly helpful when you're already struggling with the temperature.
You obviously shouldn't take risks simply to avoid a traffic jam, but when planning a longer ride it can be worth choosing a quieter route rather than spending an hour crawling through town.
If you do get stuck in traffic, take the opportunity to drink when it's safe to do so and be aware of how quickly the heat is affecting you.
7. Know the warning signs of heat exhaustion
Heat exhaustion doesn't necessarily arrive with an obvious warning. You can go from feeling slightly uncomfortable to feeling genuinely unwell without realising quite how quickly it's happened.
Dizziness, headaches, excessive tiredness, muscle cramps, nausea and difficulty concentrating are all signs that you need to take the heat seriously.
If you start experiencing these symptoms while riding, don't try to push on to your destination. Find somewhere safe to stop, get out of the sun, remove your helmet and excess layers and cool yourself down. Get some fluids onboard and give yourself time to recover.
If you're still feeling unwell after stopping and cooling down, don't get back on the bike.
Your destination can wait.
8. Slow down and don't fight the conditions
Hot weather can make for fantastic riding, but there's no reason to turn every sunny day into a race.
Riding quickly requires more concentration and physical effort, and both can contribute to fatigue when you're already dealing with high temperatures. A more relaxed pace can help you conserve energy, spot hazards earlier and enjoy the ride rather than constantly thinking about how hot you are.
It's also worth remembering that hot weather doesn't automatically mean perfect road conditions. Road surfaces can become extremely hot, tyres can behave differently, and the combination of glare, heat and fatigue can make riding more demanding than it initially appears.
So take it easy. There's no need to hurry when the weather is this good.
When is it too hot to ride a motorcycle?
There isn't a single temperature at which riding a motorcycle suddenly becomes unsafe. How you cope with heat will depend on the temperature, humidity, your riding gear, the length of the journey and how acclimatised you are to the conditions.
The important thing is to pay attention to how you're feeling.
If you're becoming dehydrated, struggling to concentrate or showing signs of heat exhaustion, the temperature has effectively become too hot for you to continue riding safely, regardless of what the thermometer says.
Hot-weather motorcycling should be enjoyable. Stay hydrated, wear the right protective gear, use the ventilation available to you, take regular breaks and don't ignore the warning signs from your body.
The best summer ride isn't necessarily the one that takes you furthest. It's the one where you arrive home feeling as good as when you left.
Simon (AKA Toad) has been working within the motorcycle industry for more than twelve years, and a member of the motorcyclist family since birth. Growing up around British-built single and twins, it was inevitable that a life on two wheels was on the cards, from a very early age!

Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 Released on a New Platform - Developer Ported the Game with AI
News
12 Aug 14:01
Recently, players remembered Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 again. A native port for Apple devices – iPad and iPhone – has been released. However, this is not an official release from Electronic Arts, but an unofficial project made possible by the development of artificial intelligence technologies.
Developer Ammaar Reshi decided to use AI tools again to create a new version of the game. He explained that EA did not publish the source code for Red Alert 2, so he had nothing to “port.”
I used Fable 5 to port Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 along with Yuri’s Revenge to iPhone and iPad! Electronic Arts never released the RA2 source code, so there was nothing to “port.” Gemini 3.6 Flash spent hours testing the game, and GPT-5.6 Sol re-implemented the AI for “Skirmish” mode.
The new version of Red Alert 2 was based on another fan project, “Chrono Divide” – a version of the game that Alexandru Ciucas recreated from scratch in TypeScript.
The developer said that AI played Red Alert 2 for a long time and helped him identify errors in the in-game AI's operation:
I connected to the project through a Chinese fork, so when I started working, the entire interface was in Chinese. Approximately 127 thousand lines of the game engine were not written by me. My personal contribution: a Swift/WKWebView shell, English translation of Yuri’s Revenge, touch screen controls, and AI created based on the Supalosa bot.
The project “RedAlert2-Mac-iOS-iPadPublic” is published open source on GitHub.
Earlier, modern technologies helped with the porting of another game in the franchise – this summer, Command & Conquer: Generals Zero Hour reached Apple devices. This is also a project by Ammaar Reshi.

articles.full_text:
TULSA, Okla. -EMSA has issued its third Medical Heat Alert of 2026 after an increase in heat-related emergency calls in the Tulsa area.
EMSA paramedics responded to nine suspected heat-related illness calls Tuesday. Seven of those patients were transported to local hospitals for further evaluation and treatment.
Since Aug. 1, EMSA has responded to 50 heat-related illness calls in the Tulsa service area and transported 33 patients to local hospitals because of heat-related complications.
EMSA urges residents to take precautions
With dangerous temperatures expected to continue, EMSA is urging residents to take steps to prevent heat-related illnesses.
People spending time outdoors should:
- Drink plenty of water and electrolyte-replacement beverages before and during prolonged outdoor activity.
- Wear lightweight, loose-fitting, light-colored clothing and a wide-brimmed hat.
- Take frequent breaks in shaded or air-conditioned areas.
- Avoid alcohol and limit caffeine, which can contribute to dehydration.
- Use air conditioning whenever possible during extreme heat.
- Visit a cooling center or public indoor space, such as a library, community center or shopping mall, if air conditioning is not available at home.
- Work outdoors with a partner and check on elderly neighbors, friends and family members.
- Carry a cell phone when outdoors so help can be called quickly if symptoms develop.
When EMSA issues a Medical Heat Alert
EMSA issues a Medical Heat Alert when paramedics respond to five or more heat-related illness calls within a 24-hour period.
The alert will remain in effect until temperatures and/or heat-related call volume decrease significantly.

Yorkshire Water has urged people to "use water wisely" during the current hot weather as the company prepared for what it said would be a "significant increase" in usage.
Recent hot and dry spells had seen increased demand on water supply, with the latest heatwave expected to bring temperatures of over 30C, the firm said.
There had been 39 days this summer where usage had been over 1.4 billion litres a day - the highest number of days above that amount on record - with that figure expected to be exceeded this week, according to Yorkshire Water.
Debbie Feldhaus, from the company, said: "We are also asking everyone to play their part, use water wisely and save it where possible."
Yorkshire Water said previous heatwaves had seen an increase of 220 billion litres of water used compared to the average - which was equivalent to the combined daily usages of Halifax, Harrogate and Leeds.
Yorkshire Water said small steps by individuals and households could reduce water usage and alleviate pressure on the wider network.
Those included taking shorter showers instead of running a bath, along with using a watering can or water butt rather than a hosepipe when watering plants.
Meanwhile, the firm said that running washing machines and dishwashers only when full and turning taps off when brushing teeth were other methods to save water.
Using a carafe when wanting a glass of water, instead of running the tap, was another way to stem water usage during hot weather, the company advised.
Feldhaus, head of strategic water resources and regional planning, said: "This is the fifth heatwave of the summer, and we know that when temperatures rise, so does demand for water.
"With temperatures set to rise above 30 degrees in the region, we're preparing for a significant increase in water usage, which will put pressure on our network.
"Our teams are working hard to manage supplies and ensure we can continue providing a reliable supply to our customers, but we are also asking everyone to play their part, use water wisely, and save it where possible. Small changes can make a big difference."
'All-time highs'
Yorkshire was now "in prolonged dry weather status, reflecting the hot, dry spring and summer we've had in the region", Feldhaus said.
"Our reservoir stocks are higher than they were at this time last year, but with water demand at all-time highs and no sign of significant rain in the forecast, it is important we all try to make small changes to our water use habits."
Last month, the firm said its reservoirs were 75% full, over 20% fuller than July last year, and it was not expected that a hosepipe ban would be introduced this summer.
Yorkshire Water's most recent figures showed reservoir stocks now stood at at 58%, above the 42.1% they were at this stage in 2025, but well below the average 73.9% for this time of year.
More than 70% of England is now officially in drought, after the nation recorded its driest July since records began in 1836.
A total of 45 million people are now living in a drought-hit area in England, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.
